title: Remainder Theorems (Chinese, Fermat's)
tagline: Year 3 — Modular arithmetic, Fermat's little theorem, Euler's theorem and the Chinese remainder theorem

introduction.overview: Remainder problems ask for the remainder when a very large number (a power, a product, a factorial) is divided by a small number. Modular arithmetic lets you replace numbers by their remainders at every step. Three theorems shorten the work: Fermat's little theorem for prime moduli, Euler's theorem for general moduli, and the Chinese remainder theorem for combining conditions on different moduli.
introduction.placementRelevance: Remainder-theorem questions are commonly asked in the hardest quantitative items of company aptitude rounds, often in the form "remainder when 2^100 is divided by 7".
introduction.realWorldContext: Check digits, hash functions, calendar calculations and public-key cryptography all use modular arithmetic.

learningObjectives: Reduce sums, products and powers modulo n
Use Fermat's little theorem aⁿ⁻¹ ≡ 1 (mod p)
Combine congruences with the Chinese remainder theorem
Use Wilson's theorem and remainders of factorials

prerequisiteKnowledge.quickRefresher: a ≡ b (mod n) means n divides a − b. If a leaves remainder r when divided by n, then a ≡ r (mod n).

coreDefinitions: a ≡ b (mod n): a and b leave the same remainder on division by n.
Fermat's little theorem: if p is prime and p does not divide a, then a^(p−1) ≡ 1 (mod p).
Euler's theorem: if gcd(a, n) = 1 then a^φ(n) ≡ 1 (mod n).
Wilson's theorem: (p − 1)! ≡ −1 (mod p) for prime p.
Chinese remainder theorem: congruences x ≡ r₁ (mod m₁) and x ≡ r₂ (mod m₂) with co-prime moduli have a unique solution modulo m₁m₂.
conceptExplanation.theoreticalIntuition: Remainders behave like numbers on a clock face of size n. Adding, multiplying and raising to a power on the clock face gives the same remainder as doing it with the big numbers first. Powers on a clock go round in cycles, and the theorems tell you how long the cycle is.
conceptExplanation.visualOrMentalModel: Reduce the base first (find its remainder), find the cycle length of the powers (using the theorem or by listing), reduce the exponent modulo the cycle length, and compute the small power.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Chinese remainder
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: x ≡ r₁ (mod m₁), x ≡ r₂ (mod m₂), gcd(m₁, m₂) = 1 → x unique mod m₁m₂

mainNarrative: Work modulo n at every step. To find 7^100 mod 5, reduce 7 to 2, so the question is 2^100 mod 5. By Fermat, 2⁴ ≡ 1 (mod 5), and 100 is a multiple of 4, so the remainder is 1.
When the modulus is not prime, find the cycle by listing powers or use Euler. Powers of 2 modulo 7 are 2, 4, 1 and then repeat with period 3. Since 100 = 3 × 33 + 1, 2^100 ≡ 2¹ = 2 (mod 7).

For factorials, use the fact that n! contains every factor up to n. For n at or above the modulus (or above the largest prime factor needed) the factorial is divisible by the modulus, so the remainder is 0. For prime p, Wilson's theorem gives (p − 1)! ≡ −1.

For two conditions with co-prime moduli, list numbers satisfying the larger modulus until one satisfies the other. x ≡ 3 (mod 5) gives 3, 8, 13, …; the first with x ≡ 2 (mod 3) is 8, so x ≡ 8 (mod 15).
A useful trick: a number that leaves remainder r on division by each of several divisors is LCM(divisors) × k + r.

deepDiveAspects.title: Negative remainders
deepDiveAspects.content: Working with −1 is often easier than with n − 1. 99 ≡ −1 (mod 100), so 99^101 ≡ (−1)^101 = −1 ≡ 99 (mod 100).

solvedExamples.title: Power by cycle
solvedExamples.question: Find the remainder when 2¹⁰⁰ is divided by 7.
solvedExamples.commonTrap: Using the cycle length 4 from other bases.

solvedExamples.title: Fermat's theorem
solvedExamples.question: Find the remainder when 3¹⁰⁰ is divided by 11.
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: The exponent 100 is a multiple of 10.
solvedExamples.commonTrap: Applying Fermat with modulus 11 but exponent 11.

solvedExamples.title: Chinese remainder
solvedExamples.question: Find the smallest positive number that leaves remainder 2 when divided by 3 and remainder 3 when divided by 5.
solvedExamples.commonTrap: Taking the sum of the two remainders.

traditionalVsShortcut.traditionalMethod: Compute the huge power and divide.
traditionalVsShortcut.shortcutMethod: Reduce the base, find the cycle length (Fermat/Euler or listing), reduce the exponent, and compute the small power.

commonMistakes.mistake: Applying Fermat to a composite modulus
commonMistakes.howToAvoid: Fermat needs a prime modulus; use Euler otherwise.

commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Using the theorem when a and n share a factor.
Taking the exponent mod n instead of mod the cycle.

placementTips.eliminationTechnique: A remainder must be less than the divisor; discard larger options.
placementTips.questionSelectionAdvice: Always check whether the base is ±1 modulo n.
placementTips.recruiterInsight: Remainder problems are the base of cycle problems in unit digits.

easy.question: The remainder when 2¹⁰⁰ is divided by 7 is
easy.explanation: 2 has cycle length 3 modulo 7 (2, 4, 1). 100 leaves remainder 1 on division by 3, so the remainder is 2.

easy.question: The remainder when 7¹⁰⁰ is divided by 5 is
easy.explanation: 7 ≡ 2 (mod 5) and 2⁴ ≡ 1. 100 is a multiple of 4, so the remainder is 1.
